Este es el primer tema del curso y no da: This is the first topic of the course and it takes nothing for granted. In it you learn to say precisely when a sentence is true, to combine sentences with “and”, “or”, “not” and “if… then”, and to negate them without slipping up. Everything that comes later —sets, proofs, even probability— uses exactly these pieces.
Antes de contar, antes de sumar, antes d: Before counting, before adding, before any number at all: what does it mean for something to be true? Mathematics is not a heap of formulas, it is a building of statements that hold one another up. This block is about the mortar.
Una <strong>proposición</strong> es una: A proposition is a sentence that is either true or false, but not both and not neither.
«¿Qué hora es?» — es una pregunta: “What time is it?” — it is a question
«¡Cierra la puerta!» — es una orden: “Shut the door!” — it is an order
«Todo par mayor que 2 es suma de dos pri: “Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes”

«Esta frase es falsa» — se contradice: “This sentence is false” — it contradicts itself
Esa última fila es la <em>paradoja del m: That last row is the liar paradox, and it is no game: paradoxes of that kind forced mathematics to be rebuilt from the ground up in the early twentieth century. You will meet it again in [[av-infinito|the topic on infinity]].
Una frase que rompe el sistema: A sentence that breaks the system
Con proposiciones simples se construyen: From simple propositions you build more complex ones using connectives. The good news is that the truth value of the result depends only on the values of the parts, and that can be tabulated exhaustively.

El «o» de las matemáticas es <strong>inc: The “or” of mathematics is inclusive: “$p \lor q$” is also true when both hold. In everyday English “coffee or tea” usually excludes, but in logic exclusion has to be stated explicitly.
Una <strong>tabla de verdad</strong> rec: A truth table runs through every possible combination of the simple propositions —with $p$ and $q$ that is four rows— and says what comes out in each. Depending on what comes out, the formula gets a name: if it is true in every row it is a tautology (a law of logic), if it is false in every row it is a contradiction, and if it depends on the row it is a contingency.
Elige una fórmula y mira su tabla comple: Pick a formula and look at its complete table. True rows are marked in green: if all of them are, the formula is a tautology.
De las cuatro filas de $p \\to q$, ¿cuán: Of the four rows of $p \to q$, how many do you think will come out true? And of $p \lor \neg p$? Commit to a number before you look.
Ni tautología ni contradicción: su verda: Neither a tautology nor a contradiction: its truth depends on $p$ and $q$.
Hay dos reglas para negar que se usan co: There are two rules for negating that get used constantly and that almost everybody applies wrongly in ordinary speech. Think of the sentence “it is raining and it is cold”. How is it negated? Many people answer “it is not raining and it is not cold”, and that is wrong: for the original sentence to be a lie it is enough that one of the two things fails. The correct negation is “it is not raining or it is not cold”. When you negate, “and” turns into “or” and the other way round.
En palabras: <em>«no es cierto que lluev: In words: “it is not the case that it is raining and cold” is the same as “either it is not raining or it is not cold”. When you negate, “and” turns into “or” and the other way round. It is one of the most useful rules there is, and it will come back in sets and in probability.
¿Cuál es la negación de «he aprobado mat: What is the negation of “I passed maths and I passed physics”?

Es lo mismo que la primera opción, dicho: That is the same as the first option, said another way: it demands two fails, when one is enough.
Una tabla de verdad no es un ejercicio d: A truth table is not a classroom exercise: it is the blueprint of a circuit. Inside any processor there are billions of AND, OR and NOT gates made of transistors, and what they do is exactly what you have just filled in on those tables. The same happens every time you filter: searching for “flat AND (Madrid OR Barcelona) AND NOT ground floor” you are writing a compound proposition, and the search engine evaluates it just as you do.
Ese plano se puede montar. En [[maq-puer: That blueprint can be built. In [[maq-puertas|the machines and languages block]] the same connectives are written as a circuit and tested with switches, and a result appears that cannot be seen from here: a single gate is enough for all of them. With “not (a and b)” repeated you can build “not”, “and” and “or”, and that is why chips are manufactured from one single piece repeated a billion times.
De la tabla al circuito: From the table to the circuit
$p \\to q$ es la conectiva más important: $p \to q$ is the most important connective and the worst understood. It is false in one case only: when $p$ is true and $q$ false. If $p$ is false, the implication is true whatever happens.

Este es el <strong>único</strong> caso e: This is the only case in which the promise is broken.

A partir de $p \\to q$ se forman otras t: From $p \to q$ three other propositions are formed, and telling them apart is essential:
¿Equivale a la original?: Is it equivalent to the original?
«Si llueve, la calle está mojada» es cie: “If it rains, the street is wet” is true. Its converse, “if the street is wet, it is raining”, is not (the water lorry may have gone by). Its contrapositive, on the other hand, “if the street is not wet, it is not raining”, is necessarily true. That equivalence is what makes proof by contraposition possible.
Confundir una implicación con su recípro: Confusing an implication with its converse is the commonest logical error there is
Con $p$ verdadera y $q$ falsa, ¿qué valo: With $p$ true and $q$ false, what is the value of $(p \to q) \lor \neg p$? You work from the inside out, one connective at a time.
Primero lo de dentro del paréntesis: $p: First what is inside the brackets: $p \to q$ with $p = T$ and $q = F$. That is exactly the one case in which an implication fails: $p \to q = F$.
Después la negación: $\\neg p$ con $p =: Then the negation: $\neg p$ with $p = T$ gives $F$.
¿Qué vale $\\neg p$ si $p$ es verdadera?: What is $\neg p$ worth if $p$ is true?
Por último, la conectiva de fuera: $F \\: Finally the outer connective: $F \lor F$. A disjunction is true only if at least one part is, so it gives $F$.
Ya tienes $F \\lor F$. ¿Verdadero o fals: You already have $F \lor F$. True or false?
El orden importa: se evalúa lo más inter: Order matters: you evaluate the innermost part first, as in an operation with brackets. With $p = F$ the result would have been $T$, because $\neg p$ would be true.

Es la contraria: se niegan las dos parte: That is the inverse: both parts are negated without swapping them. It is not equivalent, and in fact it is false (6).
Confundir una implicación con su recípro: Confusing an implication with its converse is the error that costs most dearly outside the classroom. A medical test satisfies “if you are ill, it comes out positive”; that does not mean “if it comes out positive, you are ill”. With a rare disease, most positives can be false even if the test is excellent. What is always valid is the contrapositive: “if it comes out negative, you are not ill”. You will come back to this, with numbers, in conditional probability.
«$x + 1 = 3$» no es una proposición: dep: “$x + 1 = 3$” is not a proposition: it depends on $x$. It is called a predicate, and it turns into a proposition when you quantify it, that is, when you say how many objects it is being claimed of.

La A del revés, $\\forall$, se dice «par:
The upside-down A, $\forall$, is read “for all”; the backwards E, $\exists$, is read “there exists”. They come from All and Exists, which is why they are turned round.

They read: “for all x belonging to A, P of x holds” and “there exists some x in A such that P of x”.

$P(x)$ is simply “the property being claimed of x”: it can be “is even”, “passes” or whatever is needed.
Aristóteles fundó la lógica en el siglo: Aristotle founded logic in the fourth century BC and for more than two thousand years nobody improved on it in any substantial way; Kant went so far as to write that it was finished and closed. He was wrong. In 1847 George Boole published a book with a telling title, The Mathematical Analysis of Logic, in which he turned reasoning into algebra: true was 1, false was 0, and the connectives were operations. Nobody saw any practical use for it. Ninety years later a student named Claude Shannon realised that those zeros and ones described switching circuits exactly, and wrote with that idea the most influential master's thesis in history.
Con los cuantificadores pasa lo mismo y: With quantifiers the same thing happens, and it is just as practical. To knock down the claim “all the students passed” you do not have to prove that everybody failed: it is enough to find one who failed. And to knock down “there is some student who cheated” you do have to guarantee that none did. Negating swaps the quantifier for the other one and negates what is inside.
El símbolo $\\neg$ se lee «no» y $\\equi:
The symbol $\neg$ is read “not” and $\equiv$ is read “is equivalent to”, that is, “means exactly the same”.

It says: “not, for all x, P of x, is equivalent to: there exists an x such that not P of x”.

With an example: negating “everybody passed” is not “everybody failed”, but “there is somebody who failed”. When you negate, the “for all” turns into “there exists” and the property inside is negated.
Para negar «<em>todos los cisnes son bla: To negate “all swans are white” you do not have to say that none is: a single black swan is enough. That asymmetry is enormous and it shapes the whole of mathematical practice: to knock down a “for all” one counterexample is enough; to prove it you need a general argument.
El <strong>orden importa</strong>. «$\\f: Order matters. “$\forall x\, \exists y : y > x$” is true in $\mathbb{N}$ (every number has a larger one). “$\exists y\, \forall x : y > x$” says there is a number larger than all of them, and it is false. The same words in a different order mean very different things.

Los cuantificadores son la letra pequeña: Quantifiers are the small print of contracts and of programs. “All orders are delivered within 24 h” is broken by one counterexample; “there is some free shipping” is satisfied by one. That is why negating a quantifier properly is the daily tool of anyone who tests software: to knock down a “for all” you need prove nothing, you just have to find the case that fails.
